title: didgpu
text:
Welcome to didgpu
Modern difference-in-differences work is rarely a single estimator and a single model. It is a workflow: choose an identification strategy, estimate a panel with treatment timing that may be staggered or heterogeneous, check for pre-trends, run bootstraps, compare sensitivity analyses, and often revisit trade-offs when the data become large enough to make the naive approach feel impossible.
That is where didgpu comes in.
didgpu is a GPU-capable R package for applied DiD research that brings six published estimator families under one consistent interface. It is built for researchers who want the credibility of the modern DiD literature without the pain of stitching together multiple packages, each with its own output conventions, startup costs, and idiosyncratic bootstrap behavior.
The package is designed around three principles:
A GPU is not required. Every estimator has a pure-R and Rcpp fallback, and didgpu is designed to run cleanly in both CPU-only and CUDA-enabled settings. The package is also built to behave appropriately in CRAN-style validation environments, where GPU support is not assumed.

title: didgpu
text:
0.1 Why didgpu exists
If you have used modern DiD methods in practice, you already know the frustration: the method is compelling, but the implementation story is often fragmented. Some estimators live in one package, some in another, some are only available as research code, and many demand custom workflows for bootstrap inference, sensitivity checks, and repeated runs.
didgpu consolidates the main modern DiD families into a single package with one interface, one set of conventions, and one place to compare results on the same panel.
That matters because the applied research question is often not “which one is best in the abstract?” but “which estimator is best suited to this design, and can I estimate it at scale without rewriting my workflow?”

title: didgpu
text:
0.3 What makes it practical

0.3.1 Speed where it matters
Cluster bootstrap inference is usually the dominant computational cost in modern DiD workflows. For large panels, the pure-R implementation is already credible and flexible, but the optional CUDA backend brings a substantial reduction in the time needed for repeated inference.
In benchmarked settings, the GPU path has been observed to achieve:

roughly 10x to 100x speedups for cluster-bootstrap workloads
roughly 5x to 30x speedups for the per-cell DID kernel

Performance depends on panel size, number of covariates, and the number of bootstrap replicates. See BENCHMARKS.md for the hardware and panel configurations behind these numbers.

0.3.2 Resilience for long runs
Long cluster bootstraps fail for reasons that are all too familiar: out-of-memory errors, machine restarts, interrupted jobs, or a process killed by a scheduler. Instead of forcing a complete restart, didgpu can checkpoint every completed bootstrap replicate to disk and resume from the last completed state.
This is more than a convenience feature. It is a practical reliability layer for applied work where an overnight job should not become a lost day.

0.3.3 Numerical credibility
didgpu is designed around numerical parity with the reference packages in the DiD ecosystem. Under matched settings, point estimates align to machine precision with packages such as DIDmultiplegtDYN, did, and related implementations. Analytic standard errors agree closely, and bootstrap standard errors match up to simulation noise.
This is important because performance is not the only bar. A faster estimator is not useful if it drifts materially from the benchmark software researchers use for validation.

title: 2  Installation
text:
2.1 Which install path to use
didgpu installs from CRAN in one line. Most users will not need to do anything beyond that. If you want the latest development commit, or if you have an NVIDIA GPU and want the CUDA-accelerated backend, keep reading.
The CPU backend powers all the estimators in this book and passes all tests. The GPU backend is a performance optimization for one particular estimator: large cluster bootstraps, where it can be 100-200x faster than the pure-R path. For point estimates and smaller panels, the two are usually within a few percent of each other. Install CUDA only if you are going to benefit from it.

title: 2  Installation
text:
2.2 Prerequisites
Before installing didgpu, make sure you have:

R 4.1 or newer. Check that you have it by running R --version in a terminal or R.version.string in R. If you do not have it, download it from https://cran.r-project.org.
A working C++ compiler for the Rcpp backend.
macOS: install the command line tools with xcode-select --install in Terminal.
Linux: build-essential on Debian/Ubuntu or the Development Tools group on Fedora/RHEL.
Windows: install Rtools45 from https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/. You need Rtools only when installing from source.
Optional for the GPU backend: NVIDIA CUDA Toolkit 12.0 or newer with cuBLAS and cuSOLVER.
Optional for the GPU backend: a CUDA-capable GPU with sm_75 or higher compute capability (see below).

The CUDA Toolkit can be downloaded from https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-downloads.

title: 2  Installation
text:
2.5 From source with GPU support
If you have an NVIDIA GPU and the CUDA Toolkit installed, the source install compiles the CUDA kernels.
What to expect on a Mac without CUDA. When I installed didgpu on my M1 MacBook, the configure script printed CUDA toolkit not found. Building CPU-only. right in the middle of the compiler output, and I thought the install had failed. It had not. On any Mac (and on any machine without an NVIDIA GPU), that message is the expected path: the package builds the CPU backends and skips the GPU one, and the install finishes cleanly a few seconds later with * DONE (didgpu). If you see the CUDA-not-found line and no ERROR after it, you are fine.
Step 1. Tell R where to find your CUDA installation:
# Linux
Sys.setenv(CUDA_HOME = "/usr/local/cuda")

# Windows
Sys.setenv(CUDA_PATH = "C:/Program Files/NVIDIA GPU Computing Toolkit/CUDA/v13.2")
Step 2. Install from source:
# From CRAN source
install.packages("didgpu", type = "source")

# Or from GitHub head
remotes::install_github("JoshuaAmmons/didgpu")
didgpu’s configure script emits a one-line status message at install time, telling you whether CUDA was found:
didgpu configure
CUDA toolkit detected: /usr/local/cuda
-> Building WITH GPU support.
backends available after install: 'r', 'cpu', 'cuda'
If CUDA is not found, the installation proceeds, but only the r and cpu backends are built. There is no error, warning, or message. If backend = "cuda" is called later, it will return an informative error.

title: 2  Installation
text:
2.6 Verify your install
No matter how you installed didgpu, verify that it works:
library(didgpu)
packageVersion("didgpu")
#> [1] '0.1.2'
If these two lines run without errors, the pure-R and Rcpp backends are installed.
To check whether the GPU backend is available:
didgpu_has_cuda_support()
#> [1] TRUE
A TRUE value means that you can pass backend = "cuda" to any estimator in didgpu. If you get FALSE, it means that either your system does not have CUDA installed or didgpu was not built with CUDA support.

title: 3  Quick start
text:
3.1 Generate a panel
Five minutes is enough to estimate a DiD model with didgpu. This chapter uses the package’s built-in simulator so you can reproduce every example without assembling real-world data first.
didgpu includes didgpu_simulate_panel(), which creates a tidy long panel with a known treatment effect built into the data-generating process. We use it throughout this chapter so the values you see on screen correspond directly to the examples in the text.
panel is a long-form data frame with 720 rows and four columns:
What this setup is doing:
The first six rows show unit 1 in its first six periods, all with D = 0. That is because unit 1 happens to be one of the never-treated units in this draw. Units that eventually receive treatment begin with D = 0 and switch to D = 1 at their assigned adoption period.

title: 3  Quick start
text:
library(didgpu)

panel <- didgpu_simulate_panel(
  n_units          = 60,
  n_periods        = 12,
  frac_treated     = 0.6,
  min_treat_period = 4,
  max_treat_period = 9,
  tau_profile      = c(0.5, 1.0, 1.2, 1.0, 0.8),
  sigma            = 0.4,
  seed             = 17
)

head(panel)
#>   unit period D          Y
#> 1    1      1 0 -0.3859350
#> 2    1      2 0  0.9423873
#> 3    1      3 0 -0.1117813
#> 4    1      4 0 -0.6311500
#> 5    1      5 0 -0.5164363
#> 6    1      6 0 -0.5039224

nrow(panel)
#> [1] 720


unit identifies the unit (1 through 60).
period indexes time (1 through 12).
D is the treatment indicator: 0 before treatment and 1 after treatment.
Y is the observed outcome.



60 units and 12 periods produce 720 total observations. This is small enough to run quickly, yet large enough to give the estimator meaningful variation.
60% treated means that 36 units eventually receive treatment, while 24 units remain never-treated. Those never-treated units provide the clean comparison group.
min_treat_period = 4 and max_treat_period = 9 imply that each treated unit adopts treatment at a random period between 4 and 9. Different units switch at different times, which is the staggered-adoption setting that the modern DiD estimators in didgpu are designed to handle.
tau_profile = c(0.5, 1.0, 1.2, 1.0, 0.8) is the true event-study effect. At event time 0, the effect on Y is 0.5; one period later it is 1.0; two periods later it reaches 1.2; and then it gradually decays. This is the target the estimator is meant to recover.
sigma = 0.4 adds Gaussian noise so the data look realistic rather than perfectly synthetic.
seed = 17 fixes the random draws so anyone who runs the code gets the same panel.

title: 3  Quick start
text:
3.2 Fit the dynamic DiD estimator
The primary estimator in didgpu is didgpu(), which implements the heterogeneity-robust dynamic DiD estimator of de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfoeuille (2024). For staggered-adoption designs, it estimates treatment effects at each event-time horizon after treatment while using comparisons that avoid already-treated units, the source of the bias that affects standard two-way fixed-effects regressions.
fit <- didgpu(
  panel,
  outcome   = "Y",
  group     = "unit",
  time      = "period",
  treatment = "D",
  effects   = 4,
  placebo   = 2
)
The key arguments are straightforward:

outcome, group, time, and treatment identify the four columns the estimator needs. Passing them as strings keeps the function signature aligned with DIDmultiplegtDYN::did_multiplegt_dyn().
effects = 4 requests four post-treatment event-time effects: the effect in the treatment period and in each of the next three periods.
placebo = 2 requests two pre-treatment placebo estimates. These serve as falsification tests for the parallel-trends assumption: if there is no treatment effect before treatment, the placebo estimates should be close to zero.

There is no bootstrap_reps argument in this call. Since version 0.1.2, the standard errors, confidence intervals, and joint-nullity tests are computed analytically from the estimator’s asymptotic influence functions, so a bootstrap is no longer required for default inference. Setting bootstrap_reps above zero still works, but it does not change the reported SE column. See the “When to add a bootstrap” section below for the practical guidance.

text:
3.3 Read the output
Printing the fitted object shows four blocks that match the output from DIDmultiplegtDYN line for line.

#> ----------------------------------------------------------------------
#>        Estimation of treatment effects: Event-study effects
#> ----------------------------------------------------------------------
#>              Estimate SE      LB CI   UB CI   N   Switchers
#> Effect_1     0.46833  0.11489 0.24315 0.69350 278 36
#> Effect_2     1.03675  0.10837 0.82435 1.24914 247 36
#> Effect_3     1.28974  0.11761 1.05923 1.52024 221 36
#> Effect_4     1.09481  0.08919 0.92001 1.26962 201 36
#>
#> Test of joint nullity of the effects : p-value = 0.0000
#> ----------------------------------------------------------------------
#>     Average cumulative (total) effect per treatment unit
#> ----------------------------------------------------------------------
#>  Estimate        SE     LB CI     UB CI         N Switchers
#>   0.97241   0.08404   0.80769   1.13712       458       144
#> Average number of time periods over which a treatment effect is accumulated: 2.5000
#>
#> ----------------------------------------------------------------------
#>      Testing the parallel trends and no anticipation assumptions
#> ----------------------------------------------------------------------
#>              Estimate SE      LB CI    UB CI   N   Switchers
#> Placebo_1    0.04120  0.08947 -0.13416 0.21656 278 36
#> Placebo_2    0.22337  0.10129 0.02485  0.42189 247 36
#>
#> Test of joint nullity of the placebos : p-value = 0.0640
The Effects block. Each row is a cumulative DiD estimate at one event-time horizon. Effect_1 is the effect in the treatment period, Effect_2 is the effect one period later, and so on. The N column gives the number of observations used to compute each estimate, while Switchers is the number of treated units contributing to that horizon.
Compare the estimates to the true profile built into the panel via tau_profile = c(0.5, 1.0, 1.2, 1.0, 0.8):

Every true effect lies inside its 95% confidence interval. The estimator recovers the dynamic profile within sampling error, which is exactly what we want to see on simulated data where the truth is known.
The joint-nullity test at the bottom of the Effects block tests H0: all four effects are zero. The p-value is effectively zero, so we reject the null that treatment had no effect at any horizon.
The ATE block. The row labelled “Average cumulative (total) effect per treatment unit” reports a single summary number: the switcher-weighted average effect per unit of treatment. The final line of the block, “Average number of time periods over which a treatment effect is accumulated: 2.5000”, gives the mean horizon length across switchers.
A note on interpretation: the ATE in didgpu is not simply the mean of the Effects column. It is a weighted average per unit of treatment, and the two coincide only when treatment is binary and absorbing, as it is here. In settings with multivalued or continuous treatment, the ATE denominator reflects the average treatment change among switchers, so the two quantities can diverge. The function help (?didgpu) gives the exact formula.
The Placebos block. Pre-treatment placebo estimates are a falsification test. If parallel trends holds, the placebo effects should be close to zero. Placebo_1 here is 0.04, which is comfortably near zero, while Placebo_2 is 0.22 and its confidence interval does not include zero. The joint-nullity p-value is 0.064, which is borderline.
This is an important feature even on simulated data, where the data-generating process satisfies parallel trends by construction. With finite samples, random noise can still push a placebo away from zero, and that is exactly what the test is designed to reveal. On real data, a significant placebo should prompt a careful reconsideration of whether the parallel-trends assumption is credible in the application.

title: 3  Quick start
text:
3.4 Access the fitted object
The fit is a didgpu_result object. Its structure:
class(fit)
#> [1] "didgpu_result" "list"

names(fit)
#>  [1] "coef"                 "results"              "args"
#>  [4] "cells_used"           "N_switchers_effect_1" "N_switchers_effect_2"
#>  [7] "N_switchers_effect_3" "N_switchers_effect_4" "checkpoint_dir"
#> [10] "plot"
The components you will reach for most often:

fit$results holds the three matrices (Effects, ATE, Placebos) that produce the printed output.
fit$coef holds the point estimates, their analytic covariance matrix, and the influence functions used to build it.
fit$plot is a ggplot2 object of the event-study graph (shown below).
fit$args records the arguments the call was made with. Useful for reproducibility and when you resume a long-running fit from a checkpoint.

The accessor functions covered later in this chapter are the cleaner way to pull estimates and intervals for downstream use.

title: 3  Quick start
text:
3.5 Plot the event-study estimates
Fitting the model automatically draws an event-study plot in the RStudio Plots pane. The same ggplot2 object is stored in fit$plot, which means you can redraw it, customize it, or save it to a file without re-estimating the model.
plot(fit)



didgpu event-study plot from the Quickstart fit


The horizontal axis indexes time relative to the last untreated period before treatment begins (t = 0). Negative horizons are the pre-treatment placebos (Placebo_2 at -2, Placebo_1 at -1), the point at 0 is the reference period and is fixed at zero by construction, and the positive horizons are the post-treatment effects (Effect_1 at 1 through Effect_4 at 4). The error bars show the 95% confidence intervals reported in the fit output.
Reading the plot:

The two placebo points are close to zero, but not exactly on it, which is consistent with the borderline joint-nullity p-value of 0.064 reported above.
The estimated effects rise from Effect_1 to a peak at Effect_3, then flatten. This matches the true profile tau_profile = c(0.5, 1.0, 1.2, 1.0, 0.8) used to generate the data.
The confidence intervals are wide enough to reflect sampling noise, but narrow enough that the post-treatment effects are clearly separated from zero.

To save the plot to a file for a paper or slide deck:
ggplot2::ggsave("eventstudy.png", fit$plot, width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 300)
To modify the plot, treat fit$plot as any other ggplot2 object and compose it with the usual + operator:
library(ggplot2)
fit$plot +
  labs(
    title = "Dynamic treatment effects: event study",
    y     = "Estimated effect on Y"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
To suppress the automatic draw entirely, pass graph_off = TRUE to the didgpu() call. The ggplot2 object remains available at fit$plot and can be rendered later when needed.

title: 3  Quick start
text:
3.6 Access the estimates programmatically
For downstream work, the standard accessor functions all work on a didgpu_result object. These are the main tools for extracting point estimates, uncertainty measures, and tidy summaries without manually re-parsing the printed output.
Point estimates.
coef(fit)
#>   Effect_1   Effect_2   Effect_3   Effect_4  Placebo_1  Placebo_2        ATE
#> 0.46832720 1.03674519 1.28973624 1.09481177 0.04120344 0.22337031 0.97240510
coef() returns the full named vector: the four dynamic effects, the two placebo estimates, and the ATE. You can subset by name when you want a single entry:
coef(fit)["Effect_2"]
Analytic covariance matrix.
vcov(fit)
vcov() returns the covariance matrix for the four dynamic effects and the two placebo estimates. The ATE is not a linear combination of those coefficients, so it does not appear in this matrix. If you need the variance for the ATE, use the SE column in the ATE block from fit$results$ATE.
Confidence intervals.
confint(fit)
#>                95% LB    95% UB
#> Effect_1   0.24315340 0.6935010
#> Effect_2   0.82434795 1.2491424
#> Effect_3   1.05923303 1.5202395
#> Effect_4   0.92000820 1.2696153
#> Placebo_1 -0.13415536 0.2165622
#> Placebo_2  0.02485349 0.4218871
#> ATE        0.80768812 1.1371221
These confidence intervals are the same ones reported by the original fit, at whatever level was requested in the call to didgpu() (ci_level = 95 by default). The call confint(fit, level = 0.90) does not recompute the interval at a new level; it returns the stored 95% intervals and emits a warning telling you to re-fit the model with ci_level = 0.9 if you want a different level. The intervals are computed from the analytic covariance matrix at fit time, not on demand.
Tidy data frames.
For a one-row-per-parameter data frame that is convenient for plotting or joining with other results, use didgpu_tidy():
didgpu_tidy(fit)
#>        term   estimate  std.error  statistic      p.value    conf.low   conf.high    kind
#> 1  Effect_1 0.46832720 0.11488670  4.0764265 4.573311e-05  0.24315340 0.6935010  effect
#> 2  Effect_2 1.03674519 0.10836793  9.5669005 1.101587e-21  0.82434795 1.2491424  effect
#> 3  Effect_3 1.28973624 0.11760584 10.9666001 5.531336e-28  1.05923303 1.5202395  effect
#> 4  Effect_4 1.09481177 0.08918713 12.2754452 1.227150e-34  0.92000820 1.2696153  effect
#> 5       ATE 0.97240510 0.08404082 11.5706286 5.805577e-31  0.80768812 1.1371221     ate
#> 6 Placebo_1 0.04120344 0.08947042  0.4605258 6.451388e-01 -0.13415536 0.2165622 placebo
#> 7 Placebo_2 0.22337031 0.10128595  2.2053435 2.743000e-02  0.02485349 0.4218871 placebo
The kind column distinguishes effects, the ATE, and placebo estimates, making it easy to filter or reshape the results:
library(dplyr)
didgpu_tidy(fit) |>
  filter(kind == "effect") |>
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high)
For a one-row summary of the fit, use didgpu_glance():
didgpu_glance(fit)
#>   n_effects n_placebos n_switchers_e1 n_obs_e1 p_jointeffects p_jointplacebo n_boot backend seed
#> 1         4          2             36      278              0     0.06401752      0    auto    1
A note on broom. didgpu does not currently register S3 methods with the broom package namespace, so broom::tidy(fit) and broom::glance(fit) will error with “No tidy() method recognized for this list.” The native didgpu_tidy() and didgpu_glance() functions above return the same tidy-shaped objects without introducing a broom dependency.

title: 3  Quick start
text:
3.7 When to add a bootstrap
For almost every didgpu workflow, the answer is simple: you usually do not need one. Since version 0.1.2, the standard errors, confidence intervals, and joint-nullity tests are computed analytically from the estimator’s asymptotic influence functions. The output shown earlier in this chapter already contains the valid default inference. There is no hidden step being skipped by leaving bootstrap_reps at its default value of zero.
The package makes this explicit when a non-zero bootstrap_reps value is passed:
did_multiplegt_dyn computes by default analytical standard errors -
in most cases, there is no need to use the bootstrap option.
Bootstrapping is a much slower alternative and we recommend it only
in combination with the continuous option.
In practice, running a bootstrap on the same panel confirms that it does not change the reported standard errors:
fit_boot <- didgpu(
  panel,
  outcome      = "Y",
  group        = "unit",
  time         = "period",
  treatment    = "D",
  effects      = 4,
  placebo      = 2,
  bootstrap_reps = 200,
  seed         = 42
)
cbind(
  analytic  = fit$results$Effects[, "SE"],
  bootstrap = fit_boot$results$Effects[, "SE"]
)
#>               analytic  bootstrap
#> Effect_1     0.11488670 0.11488670
#> Effect_2     0.10836793 0.10836793
#> Effect_3     0.11760584 0.11760584
#> Effect_4     0.08918713 0.08918713
The two columns are identical to every printed digit, and the point estimates are unchanged. The bootstrap still performs its resampling loop and populates a bootstrap covariance object inside fit_boot, but the SE column itself remains anchored to the analytic path.
When should you actually use it? One case is called out explicitly by the package: when continuous is set in the call to didgpu(). In that setting, the analytic standard errors can be somewhat liberal, and the bootstrap provides a more conservative alternative. The dynamic DiD chapter covers that path in more detail.
For any other workflow (binary treatment, multivalued treatment, staggered adoption, controls, or weights), leave bootstrap_reps at its default. You save minutes to hours of compute time without giving up anything in the reported inference.

title: 3  Quick start
text:
3.8 Save and reload a fit
A didgpu_result is just an R list with an S3 class attached, so saveRDS() and readRDS() work exactly as they do for any other R object.
saveRDS(fit, "quickstart_fit.rds")

fit_reloaded <- readRDS("quickstart_fit.rds")
coef(fit_reloaded)
#>   Effect_1   Effect_2   Effect_3   Effect_4  Placebo_1  Placebo_2        ATE
#> 0.46832720 1.03674519 1.28973624 1.09481177 0.04120344 0.22337031 0.97240510
The reloaded fit prints the same output, preserves the same point estimates, standard errors, covariance matrix, and confidence intervals, and remains fully compatible with the accessor functions shown above.
A note on strict object identity: if you run identical(fit, fit_reloaded), the result is FALSE, not TRUE. The numerical components round-trip exactly: identical(fit$results, fit_reloaded$results) and identical(fit$coef, fit_reloaded$coef) both return TRUE. The difference comes from the ggplot2 object stored in fit$plot: it carries environment pointers that change when the object is serialized, and identical() compares those too. Nothing in the underlying estimates or inference is affected. If you need a strict equality check in a test suite, compare the components you care about directly rather than the top-level object.
For long-running fits with bootstrap replicates or larger panels, the checkpoint system described in the “Reproducibility and checkpointing” chapter is usually a better choice than saveRDS(): it writes one cell per bootstrap replicate as the fit runs, so you can resume after a crash without redoing the full computation.

title: 3  Quick start
text:
3.9 Where to go next
You have now installed didgpu, generated a panel, fit the flagship dynamic DiD estimator, read the output, plotted the event-study graph, extracted estimates programmatically, understood when (and when not) to use a bootstrap, and saved a fit for later. This brings the quickstart to a close.
From here, three directions are especially useful depending on your application:

Choose the right estimator for your design. didgpu offers several estimator families, and the best choice depends on how treatment is defined and which identifying assumptions you are willing to make. The Choosing an Estimator chapter walks through the decision.
Go deeper on the dynamic DiD estimator. This quickstart used didgpu() with its default settings. The Dynamic DiD chapter documents every argument, covers covariates and weights, describes the diagnostic options (predict_het, effects_equal), and explains the continuous-treatment path.
Apply didgpu to other causal designs. The Callaway-Sant’Anna chapter covers staggered adoption with a clearly defined control group; the FEct, IFEct, and MC chapter covers the counterfactual-imputation family; the Static DID_M chapter covers non-absorbing binary treatment; and the Continuous treatment chapter covers settings without a clean never-treated group.

For longer-running work, the Reproducibility and checkpointing chapter explains how to resume fits after crashes, and the GPU and performance chapter covers when the CUDA backend is worth setting up and which speedups to expect.

title: 4  Choosing an estimator
text:
4.1 The six estimators
didgpu ships with six estimator families. They address closely related but substantively different problems, and the right choice depends on three practical questions:
This chapter walks through those questions in order and helps you land on the estimator that fits your application. If you already know what you want, the reference table at the end gives the function names, references, and the corresponding chapter for each estimator.
didgpu() is the heterogeneity-robust dynamic DiD estimator of de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfoeuille (2024). It handles binary, multivalued, or continuous treatment, with or without absorbing adoption, under staggered timing. It returns event-study effects at each post-treatment horizon, placebo estimates for the pre-treatment period, and a switcher-weighted average treatment effect per unit of treatment. Standard errors are analytic (influence-function based) by default, matching DIDmultiplegtDYN to machine precision. This is the workhorse estimator used in the Quickstart chapter.
didgpu_cs() is the Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) estimator. It targets ATT(g, t), the average treatment effect on the treated for each adoption cohort g at each calendar period t, under staggered adoption. It takes a control_group of either "never"-treated or "notyet"-treated units and an est_method of "OR" (outcome regression), "IPW" (inverse propensity weighting), or "DR" (doubly robust, the default). The estimator can be aggregated into event-study, calendar-time, cohort, or overall ATT estimates. Standard errors are analytic, matching did::att_gt(..., bstrap = FALSE) to machine precision. One important point is that att_gt defaults to a multiplier bootstrap with uniform confidence bands (bstrap = TRUE, cband = TRUE); didgpu’s analytic path produces pointwise intervals only.
didgpu_fect() implements the counterfactual-prediction estimators of Liu, Wang, and Xu (2024) and Athey et al. (2021). Rather than differencing treated observations against control units, it fits a model on the untreated observations and then uses that model to impute how each treated observation would have evolved without treatment. There are three methods: "fe" (two-way fixed effects), "ife" (interactive fixed effects with latent factors), and "mc" (matrix completion). Like didgpu_did_static(), it allows treatment to switch on and off. The right choice depends on how strong you expect unobserved time-varying confounding to be. Standard errors come from a cluster bootstrap with 100 replications by default; the reference fect package defaults to 200.
didgpu_did_static() is the instantaneous DID_M estimator of de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfoeuille (2020). It handles non-absorbing binary treatment and targets the instantaneous effect of switching. DID_M assumes no dynamic effects: past treatment does not affect current outcomes. If lagged effects are plausible, use didgpu(), which also handles non-absorbing treatment. Standard errors come from a cluster bootstrap with 100 replications by default.
didgpu_cs_continuous() is the continuous-treatment dose-response estimator of Callaway, Goodman-Bacon, and Sant’Anna (2024). It estimates both the dose-specific average treatment effect on the treated ATT(d) and the causal response ACRT(d) = ATT'(d) as functions of the dose, using a never-treated (zero-dose) comparison group. The implementation covers the canonical continuous-DiD design with a single treated cohort versus never-treated; staggered timing is not currently supported. Identification of ATT(d) relies on parallel trends; interpreting ACRT(d) causally requires a stronger “strong parallel trends” assumption. Standard errors come from a multiplier bootstrap with 200 replications by default.
didgpu_did_continuous() is didgpu’s implementation of a continuous-treatment DiD setting in which no units keep their dose unchanged between periods. Identification runs through quasi-stayers, units whose dose change is close to zero. The function returns effect(d) (the effect of a dose change d measured against quasi-stayers) and ACR(d) (the average causal response at change d) across a grid of dose-change values. Parametric (polynomial) and nonparametric (local-linear) estimators are available; the nonparametric path is flagged experimental in the help. Standard errors come from a multiplier bootstrap with 200 replications by default. The function cites de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfoeuille (2024); the natural reference R package for this setting is DIDHAD.
A note on standard errors across the estimator family. Since version 0.1.2, didgpu() and didgpu_cs() use analytic standard errors computed from each estimator’s influence functions, matching their reference packages to machine precision. The other four estimators still rely on bootstrap resampling. In practice, this means bootstrap_reps defaults differ by estimator: zero for didgpu() and didgpu_cs(), 100 for didgpu_fect() and didgpu_did_static(), and 200 for both continuous-treatment estimators.

title: 4  Choosing an estimator
text:
4.2 A decision guide
A practical way to choose an estimator is to work through four questions in order. Each one narrows the menu and points toward the design that best matches your application.
Question 1: Is your treatment continuous?
If the treatment is a real-valued dose (for example, concentration, tax rate, dollar amount, or hours), you need one of the two continuous-treatment estimators. The choice between them depends on whether you have a clean zero-dose comparison group.

If you have a group of units that always has zero dose and can serve as a never-treated comparison, use didgpu_cs_continuous(). It estimates the full dose-response curve ATT(d) and the causal response ACRT(d) across the observed dose range.
If no units keep their dose unchanged between periods (a HAD-style setting), use didgpu_did_continuous(), which identifies effects off quasi-stayers (units with the smallest dose changes) and reports effect(d) and ACR(d) across a grid of dose-change values.

As a rule of thumb, if you want the full dose-response curve, a zero-dose comparison group is usually important. If you only need the effect of a dose change against units that barely moved, quasi-stayer identification is often sufficient.
If the treatment is not continuous, move on to Question 2.
Question 2: Can the treatment turn off once it is on?
If treatment is strictly absorbing (once a unit is treated, it stays treated), skip to Question 3.
If treatment can switch off (for example, a policy is adopted and then repealed, a subsidy ends, or a certification lapses), you have three main options:

If you believe past treatment does not affect current outcomes (no dynamic effects), use didgpu_did_static(). It targets the instantaneous effect of switching and is the most direct estimator for this setting, but it makes the strongest assumption.
If lagged treatment effects are plausible, use didgpu(), which handles non-absorbing treatment and allows dynamics.
If you suspect strong unobserved time-varying confounding, use didgpu_fect() with method = "ife" or "mc". These estimators impute counterfactuals from a factor model rather than relying on parallel trends in levels.

Question 3: Is your treatment staggered across units?
If every treated unit adopts in the same period (or there is only one treated unit), classical two-period DiD is usually enough and you do not need didgpu. Any standard regression package can handle that case.
If units adopt at different periods, you have two main routes:

didgpu() is the dCDH dynamic estimator. It gives you an event-study profile with analytic standard errors that match DIDmultiplegtDYN and is the fastest default workflow in didgpu.
didgpu_cs() is the Callaway-Sant’Anna estimator. It gives you a grid of ATT(g, t) estimates with multiple aggregation options (event-study, group, calendar, or overall) and matches did::att_gt to machine precision under the relevant settings. Choose it when you want an explicit cohort-by-period decomposition.

If you expect strong unobserved time-varying confounding under either approach, consider didgpu_fect() as a robustness check.
Question 4: Which identifying assumption is credible in your setting?
The estimators above all require some version of parallel trends to identify a causal effect, but they differ in what they allow.

didgpu() and didgpu_cs() assume parallel trends in levels, conditional on covariates if you include them. This is the most common assumption in applied DiD.
didgpu_fect() with method = "ife" or "mc" relaxes this requirement: a violation of parallel trends can be absorbed by a small number of latent factors.
didgpu_did_static() adds the stronger assumption that there are no dynamic effects.
The two continuous estimators assume parallel trends in first differences. didgpu_cs_continuous() assumes parallel trends between dose levels and the zero-dose comparison group. didgpu_did_continuous() assumes parallel trends between units with different dose changes, with identification running through units whose dose change is close to zero. The causal-response quantities (ACRT(d) and ACR(d)) require stronger parallel-trends assumptions than their level counterparts.

Pick the weakest identifying assumption that is credible in your application. If parallel trends is clearly implausible and cannot be captured by a small number of latent factors, no estimator in didgpu will rescue that design; a different research design is needed.

title: 4  Choosing an estimator
section: 4.4 When to prefer didgpu over the reference R packages
text:
4.4 When to prefer didgpu over the reference R packages
didgpu is a reimplementation of six published estimator families, with two practical advantages over the reference packages: GPU acceleration when it is available, and per-cell checkpointing for long-running fits. The reference packages (DIDmultiplegtDYN, did, fect, DIDmultiplegt, DIDHAD, and contdid) remain the authoritative implementations of their respective methods.
didgpu’s point estimates match each reference package under matched settings, and its analytic standard errors match DIDmultiplegtDYN and did to machine precision. Bootstrap standard errors agree up to simulation noise, since bit-for-bit agreement would require identical resampling draws.
Reach for didgpu when:

You have a large panel and the cluster bootstrap is the bottleneck for an estimator that defaults to bootstrapping (didgpu_fect(), didgpu_did_static(), or either continuous estimator). Published benchmarks on an RTX 4000 Ada laptop GPU report the CS cluster bootstrap running 100 to 200 times faster than the pure-R path for panels with 40 to 200 units and 8 to 12 periods; see BENCHMARKS.md in the package repository for the benchmark specifications.
You expect a long-running fit that might be interrupted partway through (for example, by a crash, out-of-memory conditions on a cluster, or an operating system restart). didgpu writes one small file per bootstrap replicate as it runs, so a relaunch can resume from where it left off instead of restarting from scratch.
You want to compare multiple estimators on the same panel through one consistent interface. The reference packages use different conventions for column names, argument ordering, and output structure; didgpu’s estimators share a common interface inspired by DIDmultiplegtDYN.

Reach for the reference packages when:

You want the authoritative numerical reference, especially in a publication. If you are the first to report an estimate on a given dataset, the reference package often carries more weight with reviewers who are already familiar with it.
You need features that didgpu does not expose. The reference packages often provide ancillary helpers, such as specialized plotting or aggregation tools, beyond the core estimator itself.
You are already deep in a did or fect workflow and the marginal benefit of didgpu’s speed does not justify learning a new interface.

For most applied workflows, the sensible path is to start with didgpu for speed and consistency, confirm the headline numbers against the reference package once at the end, and report the reference-package numbers in the paper (or cite both).

title: 5  Dynamic DiD — didgpu()
text:
6 Dynamic difference-in-differences — didgpu()
didgpu() implements the heterogeneity-robust event-study DiD estimator of @dechaisemartin2024dynamic. It is the flagship estimator in this package and bit-for-bit numerically equivalent to the reference R package DIDmultiplegtDYN across every commonly-used option.

title: 5  Dynamic DiD — didgpu()
text:
6.1 What it estimates
For each event-time \(k \in \{1, 2, \dots, \text{effects}\}\), the per-event-time DID is the average causal effect of being exposed to a strictly higher treatment dose for \(k\) periods relative to a clean, not-yet-switched comparison group within the same baseline-treatment cohort. The estimator pools across “switcher-in” (treatment goes up) and “switcher-out” (treatment goes down) directions via Neyman-weighted averaging.
The published Effects matrix has one row per event-time, with:


Estimate, SE, LB.CI, UB.CI — the point estimate and its inference;

N (unweighted observations), Switchers (unweighted switcher cells), N.w (weighted observation mass), Switchers.w (weighted switcher mass) — the four sample-size columns the reference reports.

A parallel Placebos matrix reports pre-treatment falsification effects at horizons \(-1, -2, \dots, -\text{placebo}\).

title: 6  Callaway-Sant’Anna — didgpu_cs()
text:
7.2 What it estimates
For each group-time \((g, t)\) with \(g\) = first-treated period and \(t\) = calendar period, the conditional ATT \(ATT(g, t) = \mathbb{E}\bigl[Y_t(1) - Y_t(0) \mid G_g = 1\bigr]\) is identified by a 2×2 DiD against either the not-yet-treated or the never-treated control group.
The package returns the full att_gt matrix, then aggregates it into the published event-study / group-time / calendar / overall quantities.

title: 6  Callaway-Sant’Anna — didgpu_cs()
text:
7.3 GPU acceleration
All three inner regressions (OR, IPW, DR) run on the GPU (src/cuda_cs_inner.cu) with per-row influence functions:

OR uses an in-thread Cholesky per (g, t) cell;
IPW / DR add a per-cell IRLS logistic propensity model that replicates stats::glm.fit to ~1e-8 (verified in tests/testthat/test-cuda-cs-wiring.R);
DR layers on the outcome-regression augmentation.

Per-cell influence functions also let the cluster and multiplier bootstrap SEs run entirely on the GPU.

9 Instantaneous DID_M — didgpu_did_static()
didgpu_did_static() implements the instantaneous, non-absorbing DiD estimator of @dechaisemartin2020twoway. Unlike most staggered-adoption methods, it allows treatment to switch on and off (non-absorbing) and is identified period-by-period without imposing an event-study structure.

title: 8  Static DID_M — didgpu_did_static()
text:
9.1 What it estimates
For each unit-period \((i, t)\) where the unit switches between \(t-1\) and \(t\), the period-over-period outcome change \(Y_{i,t} - Y_{i,t-1}\) is compared against the analogous change of same-baseline stayers (units with the same treatment value at \(t-1\) that do not switch at \(t\)). Averaging over all switch events gives the unweighted DID_M; the cluster bootstrap provides SEs.

didgpu_did_continuous() implements the no-stayers continuous-treatment DiD of @dechaisemartin2024continuous. It is for the case where the treatment dose changes for nearly every unit between \(t-1\) and \(t\) — so there is no pure control group, and identification has to come from the first-difference regression interior.

title: 9  Continuous treatment — didgpu_did_continuous()
text:
10.1 What it estimates
Two related quantities:


effect(d) — the level effect of being exposed to dose \(d\) rather than the baseline dose, at first difference.

ACR(d) — the average causal response — i.e., the derivative of effect(d) with respect to \(d\) at the population dose-density.

Both are point-identified under the assumption that \(\mathbb{E}\bigl[\Delta Y \mid \Delta D = 0\bigr]\) is recoverable from “quasi-stayers” (units with \(|\Delta D| \le h\) for some bandwidth \(h\)).

title: 9  Continuous treatment — didgpu_did_continuous()
text:
10.2 Two estimator flavours


type = "parametric" — polynomial spline in \(d\), \(\sqrt{n}\)-rate estimator. Closed-form SEs.

type = "nonparametric" — local-linear smoother with bandwidth \(h \sim n^{-2/5}\). Bootstrap SEs.

text:
11.1 When the GPU pays for itself
The fixed cost of a GPU call is non-trivial (~10 ms per kernel launch), so the breakeven point is around a few thousand panel cells or ~50 bootstrap reps, whichever comes first. Below that, the R backend is fine and sometimes faster. Above it, the GPU wins by an order of magnitude.

title: 10  GPU & performance
text:
11.2 Setup
Detailed CUDA setup instructions (Windows + Linux, including the “DLL relocation” workaround for CUDA 13) live in inst/doc/cuda_setup.md. The short version:

Install the NVIDIA CUDA Toolkit (≥ 12.0).
On Linux: nothing else.
On Windows: install Rtools45 + the MSVC Build Tools (nvcc on Windows invokes cl.exe internally), then either set CUDA_PATH or rely on the default Program Files install location.
Reinstall didgpu from source. Verify with didgpu::didgpu_has_cuda_support().

title: 10  GPU & performance
text:
11.3 Picking a backend

fit <- didgpu(panel, ..., backend = "auto")

backend = "auto" does the right thing:

If CUDA is compiled in and the panel is large enough for the GPU to win, it uses CUDA;
otherwise it falls back to the Rcpp backend (cpu);
and if that path doesn’t support a feature you asked for (controls, continuous treatment, normalized estimator), it falls back further to the pure-R backend.

You can force a backend explicitly with backend = "r", "cpu", or "cuda". The output of any backend is bit-for-bit identical on the deterministic point estimate; only the bootstrap RNG stream differs between the GPU and CPU bootstraps (the SEs converge as B → ∞).

title: 10  GPU & performance
text:
11.4 Bookkeeping: which Blackwell card?
If you have a current-generation Blackwell card (RTX PRO Blackwell, RTX 50-series), make sure you’re on didgpu ≥ 0.1.1 — earlier versions silently returned all-zero CUDA results on Blackwell because the kernels were compiled only for sm_75–sm_90. The fix added sm_120 and a compute_120 PTX fallback; this is in every release from 0.1.1 onward.






Tip



A full benchmark chapter with reproducible bench scripts and per-method profiling output is in progress.

title: 11  Sensitivity analysis
text:
12 Sensitivity analysis
didgpu ships with three sensitivity-analysis wrappers that take any fitted didgpu / didgpu_cs / didgpu_fect object and return the same robust-confidence-set output the underlying methodology papers do.

title: 11  Sensitivity analysis
text:
12.1 HonestDiD (relative magnitudes, smoothness)

hd <- didgpu_honest_did(fit, M_bar = c(0, 0.5, 1, 2))
hd
plot(hd)

Wraps [@rambachan2023more]’s HonestDiD package. The “smoothness” (\(M\)) and “relative magnitudes” (\(\bar{M}\)) restrictions both work unchanged; the FLCI variant is also available.

title: 11  Sensitivity analysis
text:
12.2 Rambachan-Roth equivalence (passes-at-delta)

eq <- didgpu_equivalence(fit, delta = 0.05, alpha = 0.05)
eq

The “equivalence-style” test reports passes_at_delta — whether the joint test rejects the null that every effect is within \(\pm\delta\) of zero.

title: 11  Sensitivity analysis
text:
12.3 Freyaldenhoven-Hansen-Shapiro pre-trend correction

fhs <- didgpu_freyaldenhoven(fit, ...)

Wraps [@freyaldenhoven2019pretrends] for trend-stable confidence sets.

title: 12  Reproducibility & checkpointing
text:
13 Reproducibility & checkpointing
didgpu’s checkpointing is the difference between a 12-hour bootstrap that resumes after a crash and a 12-hour bootstrap that has to start over.

title: 12  Reproducibility & checkpointing
text:
13.1 Turn it on

fit <- didgpu(
  panel, ...,
  bootstrap_reps = 2000,
  checkpoint_dir = "~/didgpu-runs/2026-05-28-fit",
  seed           = 17
)

didgpu writes one small RDS file per bootstrap cell (the per-rep sufficient statistics, not the panel — usually a few KB each).

title: 12  Reproducibility & checkpointing
text:
13.2 Resume after a crash
Just rerun the same call with the same checkpoint_dir and seed. didgpu reads the existing cells, picks up at the next missing one, and finishes:

fit <- didgpu(
  panel, ...,
  bootstrap_reps = 2000,
  checkpoint_dir = "~/didgpu-runs/2026-05-28-fit",  # same path
  seed           = 17                                # same seed
)

No tryCatch, no manual sharding, no “what was I up to?” archaeology.

title: 12  Reproducibility & checkpointing
text:
13.3 How “same seed = same result” works
didgpu’s bootstrap uses a deterministic per-cell seed derived from (seed, replicate_index). So:

Cells produced before the crash are bit-identical to what the resumed run would produce.
The aggregator sees a complete cell set regardless of which run wrote each one.
Bootstrap point estimate, SE, CI, and joint p-values are reproducible across crashes.

title: 12  Reproducibility & checkpointing
text:
13.4 Aggregating already-saved cells
If you want to look at a partial run without re-fitting:

partial <- didgpu_aggregate_cells(
  checkpoint_dir = "~/didgpu-runs/2026-05-28-fit"
)
partial

Returns the aggregated fit using whatever cells exist on disk. Useful for sanity-checking convergence while a long run is still going.






Tip



A worked example — deliberately interrupt a 1000-rep bootstrap, then resume it, then compare to a fresh run — is in progress.

title: 13  Bootstrap variants & clustering
text:
14 Bootstrap variants & clustering
didgpu supports two bootstrap kinds for didgpu_cs() and didgpu_fect():
For didgpu() only the cluster bootstrap is supported (the dynamic estimator’s IFs require additional work that is on the roadmap).

title: 13  Bootstrap variants & clustering
text:
14.1 Specifying a cluster
By default the bootstrap clusters on the unit:

fit <- didgpu(..., bootstrap_reps = 500)

If your unit is not the natural cluster (panel of student outcomes where the policy varies at the school level, etc.), pass cluster:

fit <- didgpu(
  panel, ...,
  cluster        = "school_id",
  bootstrap_reps = 500
)

title: 13  Bootstrap variants & clustering
text:
14.2 Resampling at multiple levels
For multi-way clustering (e.g. classroom-within-school), use a composite cluster id:

panel$cluster_composite <- paste(panel$school_id, panel$classroom_id, sep = ":")
fit <- didgpu(panel, ..., cluster = "cluster_composite", bootstrap_reps = 500)

didgpu’s resampler is a 1-pass random hash of clusters → reps, so it scales linearly in B.

title: 13  Bootstrap variants & clustering
text:
14.3 Multiplier bootstrap

cs <- didgpu_cs(
  panel, ...,
  est_method     = "DR",
  bootstrap_reps = 5000,
  bootstrap_kind = "multiplier",
  seed           = 17
)

This is the fast variant. It uses per-unit influence functions \(\psi_i\) and Rademacher / Mammen multipliers \(\xi_b\):
\[
\hat\theta^{(b)} - \hat\theta \approx \frac{1}{n} \sum_i \xi_b \, \psi_i
\]
On the GPU, all of this is a couple of GEMVs and a Cholesky per multiplier — vastly faster than refitting the inner estimator 5000 times.






Tip



A worked example comparing cluster and multiplier bootstrap SEs on the same panel (they agree to ~1e-2 at B = 2000) is in progress.

title: 14  Methodology notes
text:
15 Methodology notes
This chapter compiles the internal-implementation notes for each estimator family. It is mostly of interest to people verifying numerical equivalence with the reference packages, or porting didgpu’s algorithms to another language.

title: 14  Methodology notes
text:
15.1 Dynamic DiD — didgpu()
The estimator is described in two papers. The current implementation follows the algorithm of @dechaisemartin2024dynamic verbatim, with the following implementation notes specific to this package:

Same-switchers gate. The package’s same_switchers option applies a per-group still_switcher_XX indicator computed before the per-event-time loop. The placebo block uses the same gate (verified against DIDmultiplegtDYN 2.3.x).
Neyman pooling weight. The pooling weight \(w_\text{in} = N_\text{in}/(N_\text{in} + N_\text{out})\) uses the exact (un-floored) weighted switcher mass.
Reported sample sizes. Per-event-time, four counts are reported: N (unweighted observations), Switchers (unweighted switcher cells), N.w (weighted observation mass), Switchers.w (weighted switcher mass).
Trailing unestimable horizons. When the data-availability clamp \(\max L_g\) permits a horizon that no switcher reaches with a valid control, didgpu drops the trailing NA row to match the reference’s reported horizon count.

title: 14  Methodology notes
text:
15.2 Callaway-Sant’Anna — didgpu_cs()

Inner estimators. OR uses an in-thread Cholesky per (g, t); IPW / DR add a per-cell IRLS logistic propensity model replicating stats::glm.fit to ~1e-8.
Influence functions. Computed per-row, then aggregated per the requested aggregation (event / group / calendar / overall).
Bootstrap. Cluster and multiplier variants both supported; the multiplier variant uses per-unit IFs and is the recommended inference for large B.

title: 14  Methodology notes
text:
15.3 FEct / IFEct / MC — didgpu_fect()

IFE. Two-pass Gauss-Seidel sweep on the factor matrix, then a truncated SVD via the GPU’s cuSOLVER. CV on rank selection.
MC. Soft-impute via cuSolverDnDgesvd, with the nuclear-norm \(\lambda\) chosen by CV from a log grid.

title: 14  Methodology notes
text:
15.4 Reproducibility & seeding
didgpu’s bootstrap seed scheme is a deterministic hash(seed, replicate_index) per cell. This guarantees that:

same seed + same cells = same result
across crashes, resumed cells equal what a fresh run would produce
GPU and CPU agree on the deterministic point estimate (only the bootstrap RNG stream differs).







Tip



The internal reference notes (inst/doc/reference_internals.md) have the full algorithmic pseudo-code for each estimator. Selected sections will be inlined into this chapter as the book matures.

title: 15  FAQ
section: 16.1 Do I need a GPU to use didgpu?
text:
16.1 Do I need a GPU to use didgpu?
No. The pure-R and Rcpp backends are full citizens; everything in this book works on a laptop with no GPU. The CUDA backend is optional and detected at install time.

title: 15  FAQ
section: 16.2 My CUDA build returns all zeros — what gives?
text:
16.2 My CUDA build returns all zeros — what gives?
You’re almost certainly on a Blackwell-class card (RTX PRO Blackwell, RTX 50-series) and an older didgpu (< 0.1.1). Upgrade to didgpu ≥ 0.1.1 — those versions added sm_120 and a compute_120 PTX target.

title: 15  FAQ
section: 16.3 How long does a typical bootstrap run take?
text:
16.3 How long does a typical bootstrap run take?
For a panel of 200 units × 12 periods × 500 bootstrap reps:

backend = "r" — minutes to ~30 min depending on estimator;
backend = "cuda" (Ampere or newer) — seconds to a couple of minutes.

For larger panels the gap widens. See Chapter 8 — GPU & Performance for indicative numbers.

title: 15  FAQ
section: 16.4 My bootstrap crashed at hour 11 of 12. Do I have to start over?
text:
16.4 My bootstrap crashed at hour 11 of 12. Do I have to start over?
No. As long as you passed a checkpoint_dir and a seed, just rerun the same call. didgpu picks up at the first missing cell. See Chapter 10 — Reproducibility & checkpointing.

title: 15  FAQ
section: 16.5 Does didgpu agree with DIDmultiplegtDYN / did / fect?
text:
16.5 Does didgpu agree with DIDmultiplegtDYN / did / fect?
Yes — by design and by continuous test. didgpu’s CI runs a randomized differential-test suite of tens of thousands of panels against each reference package on every push. Current status: bit-for-bit equivalence on the deterministic point estimates and within Monte Carlo error on the bootstrap SEs (which use independent RNG streams).
The few intentional differences (always cosmetic, never inferential) are documented in NEWS.md.

title: 15  FAQ
section: 16.6 Can I use didgpu with weighted panels?
text:
16.6 Can I use didgpu with weighted panels?
Yes. Every estimator family accepts a weight = "wt_col" argument. The four sample-size columns (N, Switchers, N.w, Switchers.w) report both unweighted counts and weighted sums explicitly, so you know exactly what you’re being shown.

title: 15  FAQ
text:
16.7 How do I cite didgpu?
citation("didgpu"). didgpu also reminds you in its print output to cite the method paper for whichever estimator you ran (de Chaisemartin & D’Haultfoeuille, Callaway & Sant’Anna, Liu et al., Athey et al., as appropriate).

title: 15  FAQ
text:
16.8 Where do I report bugs?
https://github.com/JoshuaAmmons/didgpu/issues. Please include a reproducible example using didgpu_simulate_panel() or your own small panel; the package’s print methods and didgpu_glance() / didgpu_tidy() are useful for paste-into-issue summaries.

17 Changelog
The changelog is maintained in NEWS.md in the package source. The chapter below is auto-rendered from that file on every build of the docs site.

title: 16  Changelog
text:
18.1 Bug fixes

Bootstrap SEs survive partial-NA iterations. A kept bootstrap iteration can carry NA at some horizons (its resample has switchers overall but none reaching horizon j). Plain sd()/cov() then returned NA — with few switchers this silently wiped out EVERY SE, CI and joint p-value while the point estimates looked fine. Per-horizon SEs are now computed from the finite draws with a minimum bootstrap support of 30 finite draws per horizon (below that the SE stays NA, honestly), and the stored $coef$vcov uses a pairwise-complete covariance.
Joint tests: near-singular covariance now warns. With many horizons and few switchers, the bootstrap covariance behind the omnibus joint-effects/placebo chi-square can be near-singular; the statistic is then numerically unstable (tiny eigenvalues amplify arbitrary linear combinations). .joint_pvalue() now excludes horizons with inadequate bootstrap support and emits a warning when rcond(V) < 1e-10, advising a low-dimensional prespecified test (e.g. the leads nearest treatment) instead of the omnibus p.
CUDA: unbalanced panels with late-entrant groups no longer crash with error 700. Groups unobserved at the global first period have NA baseline treatment (d_sq); on the CPU path they fall out of every cohort mask and contribute zero, but on the CUDA path the NA flowed through match() into cohort_key as NA_integer_, which reaches the kernels as INT_MIN and caused an illegal memory access (CUDA DID kernel failed with code 700) in k_finalize_dist_and_kernel — and error 700 poisons the CUDA context, so every subsequent didgpu call in the process failed too. Any real-world unbalanced panel (units entering the sample over time) hit this immediately. NA-key rows are now parked in a padding cohort whose kernel contribution is identically zero, matching CPU semantics bit-for-bit. Diagnosed with compute-sanitizer (invalid 8-byte global read at base + INT_MIN * 8); regression-tested in test-cuda-late-entrants.R, including a context-not-poisoned check.
Bootstrap aggregation no longer crashes on degenerate resamples. Under sparse-switching treatments (few clean switchers), a bootstrap resample can contain no valid switcher cell at some horizon, yielding a zero-length effects vector. .aggregate_to_result()’s vapply() calls hard-required full-length vectors, so a single such iteration aborted the entire estimation with values must be length K ... result is length 0 — and because the failure probability grows with bootstrap_reps, exactly the large-rep runs users want for final inference were the ones crashing. Degenerate iterations are now dropped with a warning that reports the count; SEs and the bootstrap covariance use the surviving iterations (standard failed-resample practice). Found while re-estimating thin subsamples at 2,000 reps; e.g. a 78-DAO/4-switcher spec had 103/2,000 degenerate resamples.

title: 16  Changelog
text:
19.1 Bug fixes


CUDA: support Blackwell (sm_120) GPUs. The GPU build previously targeted only Turing–Hopper (sm_75–sm_90) with no PTX fallback, so on Blackwell parts (RTX PRO Blackwell, RTX 50xx) the kernels had no device image and effect estimates silently came back as all zeros while the CPU/R backends were correct. Added compute_120,sm_120 plus a compute_120 PTX target to both src/Makevars and src/Makevars.win. GPU effects are again bit-identical to the CPU/R backends on Blackwell (verified on an RTX PRO 5000 Blackwell, CUDA 13.2).

Windows build: ship src/didgpu_cuda.def. The DLL export list was git-ignored (/src/*.def), so clean checkouts — and the r-universe / install_github source build — could not link didgpu_cuda.dll. It is now tracked.

Windows build: locate CUDA runtime DLLs under bin/x64. CUDA 13 moved the redistributable DLLs from bin/ to bin/x64/; the bundling step now searches both so didgpu_cuda.dll loads at runtime.

title: 16  Changelog
text:
19.2 Reference parity with DIDmultiplegtDYN 2.3.x
didgpu was originally validated bit-for-bit against an older DIDmultiplegtDYN. Two of its outputs were deliberately changed upstream; didgpu now tracks the current (fixed) behavior:


predict_het standard errors now use HC2. The reference switched the heterogeneity-regression variance from HC1 to HC2 (sandwich::vcovHC(type = "HC2")) in v2.3.1 (“explicit CI formulas” fix). didgpu now does the same (new sandwich dependency), so the predict_het SE/t/LB/UB/pF columns match again.

Placebo N counts each contributing cell once. For bidirectional panels the reported placebo sample size was double-counting controls shared between the switcher-in and switcher-out comparisons. It now uses the in-direction count, matching the reference’s per-row coalesce(in, out) combiner across both in>out and out>in panels. Point estimates were never affected.

title: 16  Changelog
section: 19.3 Correctness fixes (found by randomized differential testing vs the reference)
text:
19.3 Correctness fixes (found by randomized differential testing vs the reference)


same_switchers: the placebo now uses the same restricted switcher set as the effects. Under same_switchers = TRUE the placebo block was computed on the full switcher set rather than the consistent-switchers subset, producing a biased placebo estimate (and inflated placebo N) relative to did_multiplegt_dyn. The placebo distance now honours the effects-based still_switcher restriction (the reference derives the placebo distribution from the same_switchers-gated effect distance), so placebo estimates and counts match again.

trends_lin: no longer crashes on panels with zero estimable effects. On short panels where no group has the F_g-2 pre-period that trends_lin requires, result aggregation crashed with “length of ‘dimnames’ [1] not equal to array extent” (an unguarded row-name build on a 0-row table). It now returns an empty, no-estimable- effects result cleanly.

Weighted N / Switchers columns now separate unweighted counts from weighted sums. On weighted panels (weight =) the four reported count columns were all populated from the same (weighted, truncated) switcher mass, so N / Switchers reported weighted sums instead of observation counts, and N.w lost the fractional weight (each cell’s weight was floored before summing). The estimator now reports N and Switchers as the true unweighted observation / switcher counts and N.w / Switchers.w as the (unfloored) weighted sums, matching did_multiplegt_dyn exactly. Point estimates were never affected — the weighted switcher mass that drives the Neyman pooling and ATE weights is unchanged; only the reported count columns moved. On unweighted panels all four columns coincide as before (bit-identical output).

Weighted estimates: Neyman direction-pooling no longer truncates the switcher mass. On weighted panels with switchers in both directions, the per-direction weighted switcher mass was floored to an integer before being used as the Neyman pooling weight (w_in = N_in / (N_in + N_out)) and as the across-horizon ATE weight, biasing the pooled event-study estimates by ~1e-3. The exact (unfloored) mass is now used throughout the estimate path, matching did_multiplegt_dyn. Single-direction (switchers = "in"/"out") and unweighted panels were never affected (the weight is 0/1 or the mass is already integer). Found by randomized weighted×flag differential testing.

Reported effect/placebo count: drop trailing unestimable horizons. didgpu’s horizon clamp uses each group’s own data availability (max L_g), which can be one step more permissive than did_multiplegt_dyn’s cohort-level T_g clamp. When that extra horizon has no switcher reaching it (NA estimate, zero switchers), the reference omits the row; didgpu now trims the trailing block of such unestimable effect/placebo rows so the reported horizon count matches. Estimable horizons, estimates, and all four count columns are unchanged. Verified across 359 boundary-stress panels (switchers in/out/both × effects 4–5 × weighted/unweighted): zero horizon count mismatches and, importantly, no case where didgpu reported an extra horizon with positive switchers. Found by overnight differential testing.

Placebos: drop the whole block when every horizon is unestimable. On weighted trends_lin (and other short-panel cases) the placebo block can be entirely unestimable — no group has the F_g - q - 1 pre-period any placebo horizon needs. did_multiplegt_dyn returns NULL placebos in that case; didgpu used to emit a placebo matrix of NAs. Aggregation now drops the placebo block when every placebo point estimate is NA, matching the reference. Found by extended weighted×flag differential testing (4 of 4 affected panels now match; all other scenarios untouched — verified 30 seeds × 14 scenarios = 420 weighted comparisons, 0 fails).

title: 16  Changelog
text:
20.1 Callaway-Sant’Anna (2021) — didgpu_cs()



est_method = c("OR", "IPW", "DR") — all three inner estimators. DR is Sant’Anna-Zhao (2020) doubly-robust.

control_group = c("never", "notyet") — never-treated OR not-yet-treated.

covariates = for OR/IPW/DR adjustment.
Pre-treatment placebos computed automatically; joint chi-square test on the placebo block via fit$placebo.
Four aggregations (event / group / calendar / overall) with didgpu_cs_aggregate() for switching post-fit.

bootstrap_kind = c("cluster", "multiplier") — cluster bootstrap on units, or multiplier wild bootstrap on per-unit influence functions (much faster for large B).
CUDA: all three inner regressions (OR / IPW / DR) run on the GPU (src/cuda_cs_inner.cu) with per-row influence functions. OR uses an in-thread Cholesky per cell; IPW/DR add a per-cell IRLS logistic propensity model replicating stats::glm.fit (ATT agrees with R to ~1e-8), and DR layers on the outcome-regression augmentation. With per-cell IFs, the cluster + multiplier bootstrap SEs all run on the GPU — the DR cluster bootstrap is ~192x faster than R.
Cross-validated against the reference did package on simulated panels (max abs diff < 0.25 on event-study estimates).

title: 16  Changelog
text:
20.2 TestMechs (Kwon & Roth 2026) — didgpu_test_sharp_null()


All three test methods: "CS" (Cox-Shi 2023), "ARP" (Andrews-Roth-Pakes 2023), "FSST" (Fang-Santos-Shaikh-Torgovitsky 2023).
Both binary mediator (K = 2) and multi-level (K >= 2) under no-defiers.
Generic CS engine .testmechs_cs_test(theta_hat, Sigma, A, A_eq, b_eq) is reusable for any moment-inequality test.
Nonparametric and Bayesian (Dirichlet) bootstrap of the partial-density vector beta.obs.
CUDA bootstrap kernel src/cuda_testmechs_bootstrap.cu (cuRAND multinomial; the main acceleration target). Live on Linux/WSL and wired through .testmechs_bootstrap_cuda; the “nonparametric” method runs on the GPU, “bayes” uses the R path. cuRAND vs R’s MT19937 differ per-replicate, so bootstrap moments match within Monte-Carlo error rather than bit-for-bit.

title: 16  Changelog
text:
20.3 Leave-one-out robustness — didgpu_loo()


Drops one entity at a time (cohort / unit / cluster / arbitrary column level) and re-fits the estimator.
Works on all three estimator families: didgpu_result, didgpu_cs_result, didgpu_fect_result.
Returns a didgpu_loo_result data.frame with leave_out, estimate, delta, and delta_pct columns, sorted by abs(delta) descending so the most-influential drop is on top.

print() shows the top-N most influential rows with an interpretation hint; plot() draws a tornado plot of deltas.
Default by = "cohort" (leave-one-cohort-out, the standard DiD diagnostic). Pass by = "unit", "cluster", or any column name to drop on a different key.

title: 16  Changelog
text:
20.4 HonestDiD (Rambachan & Roth 2023) — didgpu_honest_did()


Sensitivity analysis on event-study DiD estimates.

method = c("RM", "M") — relative-magnitudes OR smoothness bounds.
Reports the breakdown parameter (smallest Mbar at which the CI includes zero) so users can read off how robust their conclusion is.
Works on both didgpu_result (DIDmultiplegtDYN-style) and didgpu_cs_result (Callaway-Sant’Anna) fits.

title: 16  Changelog
text: 20.5 fect family (counterfactual-prediction estimators) — didgpu_fect()

title: 16  Changelog
text:
20.6 Estimator (bit-identical to DIDmultiplegtDYN::did_multiplegt_dyn)

Binary, multivalued, and continuous treatment.

effects, placebo, switchers = ""/"in"/"out", ATE.

weight, controls, trends_nonparam cohort extension.

only_never_switchers, same_switchers, dont_drop_larger_lower.

normalized = TRUE (per-unit-of-treatment), trends_lin = TRUE (linear cohort trends with cumulative-recovery placebos).

same_switchers_pl (placebo-side same-switchers gate; mirrors the reference’s constraint that it must be paired with same_switchers).

predict_het (heterogeneity regression with HC1 robust SEs and joint F-test).

didgpu_by_path() for treatment-trajectory subgroup analysis (the equivalent of the reference’s by_path argument).
Sample-size columns (N, Switchers, N.w, Switchers.w) match the reference exactly.

didgpu_equivalence(fit, delta) — pre-trends equivalence (TOST) test on the placebo estimates. Instead of “failed to reject a zero pre-trend” (weak, and worst exactly when underpowered), it tests H0: |pre-trend| >= delta and REJECTING is positive evidence the pre-trend is within +/- delta. Reports per-horizon and joint (intersection-union) verdicts plus the smallest defensible margin (breakdown_delta). Mirrors didgpu_fect_equivalence().

didgpu_joint_placebo(fit, horizons) — the joint chi-square placebo test (p_jointplacebo) restricted to a chosen pre-treatment window, reusing the stored bootstrap covariance. Test parallel trends only over the leads you care about; the full-window call reproduces the headline p_jointplacebo exactly.

didgpu_bacon() — Goodman-Bacon (2021) decomposition of the static TWFE DiD into its 2x2 timing-group comparisons, with the total weight on “forbidden” already-treated-control comparisons as the bias diagnostic. Validated by the exact identity (weighted 2x2 sum == the TWFE coefficient from didgpu_twfe()). Balanced, binary, absorbing panels.

didgpu_did_static() — de Chaisemartin & D’Haultfoeuille (2020) DID_M instantaneous estimator. Unlike the staggered-adoption methods it allows treatment to turn on AND off (non-absorbing): it compares each switcher’s period-over-period outcome change to same-baseline stayers and averages over all switch events, with a cluster bootstrap SE. Native reimplementation; cross-checked against DIDmultiplegt::did_multiplegt.

didgpu_freyaldenhoven() — Freyaldenhoven, Hansen & Shapiro (2019) pre-event panel event study. estimator = "OLS" is the two-way FE event study; estimator = "FHS" adds an auxiliary proxy covariate as an endogenous regressor and 2SLS-instruments it with a far policy lead to purge a confound that generates pre-trends. Native reimplementation of the first-difference parameterization; coefficients match eventstudyr::EventStudy (OLS and FHS) to machine precision.

didgpu_cs_continuous() — Callaway, Goodman-Bacon & Sant’Anna (2024) difference-in-differences with a CONTINUOUS treatment (dose). Estimates the dose-response curve: the level effect ATT(d) and the causal response ACRT(d) = ATT’(d), via a B-spline regression of the within-unit outcome change on the dose, vs a never-treated comparison; multiplier-bootstrap SEs. Native reimplementation (spline basis via splines2); ATT(d)/ACRT(d) match contdid::cont_did exactly.

didgpu_did_continuous() — de Chaisemartin & D’Haultfoeuille (2024) continuous treatment with NO STAYERS. When the dose changes for (almost) every unit there is no pure control group, so identification is in first differences: with dY, dD the within-unit changes, the common trend E[dY|dD=0] is recovered from quasi-stayers (dD near 0), giving the level effect effect(d) = E[dY|dD=d] - E[dY|dD=0] and the average causal response ACR(d). estimator = "parametric" fits a polynomial in dD (sqrt(n)); estimator = "nonparametric" is a local-linear (kernel) fit (n^2/5; flagged EXPERIMENTAL — no maintained R reference exists to bit-validate it). Multiplier-bootstrap SEs. Both estimators validated by simulation against a known dose-response.
All eight auxiliary estimators above were benchmarked to verify they belong on the CPU (none has a GPU-amenable hot path; see BENCHMARKS.md). The audit also caught and fixed two quadratic bootstraps: didgpu_did_static’s cluster bootstrap was O(n_units^2) per replicate (pre-splitting by cluster makes it O(n); 12-23x faster, bit-identical SEs), and didgpu_did_continuous no longer recomputes the O(n^2) overall-ACR on every bootstrap replicate (nonparametric bootstrap ~675x faster; reported effect(d)/ACR(d) unchanged).

title: 16  Changelog
text:
20.8 Backends


"r" — pure R via data.table. 60× faster than the reference at 200 K rows.

"reference" — delegate to DIDmultiplegtDYN::did_multiplegt_dyn, used as the parity oracle.

"cuda" — live on Windows and Linux/WSL2 (built + verified end-to-end on an NVIDIA RTX 4000 Ada, CUDA 12.6; bit-identical results on both). On Windows it needs no admin rights: a user-local CUDA toolkit plus a two-DLL split (didgpu_cuda.dll built by nvcc/MSVC, the R-facing didgpu.dll built by Rtools/MinGW, bridged by a pure-C ABI) sidesteps the MinGW↔︎MSVC link barrier — see WINDOWS_BUILD_STATUS.md. Live GPU paths: the CS cluster bootstrap (179–228× faster than R via the influence-function shortcut), the CS multiplier bootstrap, the CS OR point estimate (bit-exact vs R), and the TestMechs nonparametric bootstrap. The fect SVD path is size-gated — it only engages for very large balanced panels, since cuSOLVER loses to CPU LAPACK on the small matrices typical of fect. Every GPU path falls back transparently to R when CUDA is unavailable or would be slower, so backend = "cuda" is always safe. See BENCHMARKS.md and tests/testthat/test-cuda-equivalence-grid.R (142 lock-step assertions). Tests skip GPU paths when nvcc / a device is absent.

"cpu" — Rcpp+Eigen, scaffolded only.

title: 16  Changelog
text:
20.10 fect family (counterfactual-prediction estimators)


didgpu_fect(method = "fe") — two-way fixed effects, iterative demeaning of the controls-only outcome matrix.

didgpu_fect(method = "ife") — Bai (2009) interactive fixed effects. Alternating fe-step + rank-r SVD of the residual matrix until convergence.

didgpu_fect(method = "mc") — Athey et al. (2021) matrix completion. Iterative soft-thresholded SVD on the controls-only matrix.
All three reuse didgpu()’s checkpoint / resume / parallel bootstrap infrastructure. Results are returned as didgpu_fect_result (extends didgpu_result) so all the standard accessors (coef, confint, vcov, plot, tidy, glance) work the same way.
CUDA kernels for fect live in src/cuda_fect_fe.cu and src/cuda_fect_svd.cu (the latter uses cuSOLVER’s cusolverDnDgesvdj for the SVD primitive shared by ife and mc) and are wired through R. However, they are size-gated: on the small, tall-skinny matrices typical of fect panels the per-iteration cuSOLVER SVD is 100–300× slower than R’s LAPACK (cuSOLVER handle + H2D/D2H overhead dwarfs the tiny SVD). .fect_cuda_svd_worthwhile() only routes to the GPU for very large balanced panels (n_units ≥ 2000 and n_units·n_periods ≥ 2e5); below that backend = "cuda" transparently uses R’s svd(). See BENCHMARKS.md.

title: 16  Changelog
text:
20.12 Validation


Monte Carlo CI coverage by switcher count (tools/validation/): with the cluster bootstrap, 95% CIs achieve ~94% coverage at 8+ switchers, ~87% at 4, but only ~66% at 2 — the classic few-treated-clusters failure, not specific to didgpu. Point estimates are unbiased at every count. Practical rule: treat estimates identified off fewer than ~5 clean switchers as diagnostics; their bootstrap CIs materially undercover. The degenerate-resample drop does not distort coverage where support is adequate (8-13 switchers: nominal).
